name: Secure Sharing Practices

quiz.text: What was the root cause of the data exposure in this exercise?

answers.text: The SecureShare platform had a security vulnerability
Alice used Full Control, 'Anyone with the link', no expiration, and no password on a confidential document
Marcus gave Alice the wrong instructions
The auditor's email account was hacked

quiz.text: What is the recommended default permission level when sharing a file externally?

answers.text: Full Control — so recipients can do whatever they need
Edit — most people will need to make changes
View Only — start with minimum access and upgrade only if needed
Anyone with the link — it's the easiest option

quiz.text: Why should shared links always have expiration dates?

answers.text: To force people to work faster
To limit the exposure window — if a link is leaked or forwarded, it eventually stops working
To save server storage space
Expiration dates are optional for external shares

quiz.text: How should you share a password for a password-protected file?

answers.text: Include it in the same email as the link for convenience
Through a separate channel like a phone call or text message
Put it in the file name so the recipient knows what to type
Passwords aren't necessary if the recipient is verified

quiz.text: A colleague asks you to share a confidential file using "Anyone with the link" and no expiration because they need it shared quickly. What should you do?

answers.text: Create the link as requested since they have a valid reason
Refuse and report the colleague to management
Explain the risks and offer secure alternatives — View Only, 7-day expiration, and password protection
Create the open link but set a short expiration as a compromise

steps.name: A Busy Week at Catalyst Ventures
steps.description: Today is particularly hectic — the Q3 audit window closes at 5 PM and the external auditor still hasn't received the financial report.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Urgent Request
steps.note: Time pressure is one of the top reasons employees skip security controls. Watch how it affects Alice's sharing decisions.

telegramMessage.text: Alice — URGENT. The external auditor says they never got the Q3 financial report and their audit window closes TODAY at 5 PM. Can you share it with them ASAP through SecureShare? Their email is steve.henderson@techservices-global.com. Just get it to them fast, we can't lose this audit window.

steps.description: Alice receives an urgent message from her manager Marcus Chen on Telegram.
steps.instructions: Read Marcus's Telegram message.

steps.name: Accessing SecureShare
steps.description: Under pressure to meet the 5 PM deadline, Alice opens the Catalyst SecureShare portal to send the report as quickly as possible.
steps.instructions: Log in to the SecureShare portal using your credentials from the password manager.

steps.name: Selecting the File
steps.description: The SecureShare portal displays Alice's files. She needs to select the Q3 Financial Report to share with the auditor.
steps.instructions: Click on the Q3 Financial Report to select it for sharing.

steps.name: Setting the Recipient
steps.description: Alice needs to enter the auditor's email address from Marcus's message.
steps.instructions: Enter the recipient's email address and click Continue.

steps.name: Quick Share Settings
steps.description: The sharing configuration page appears. Alice is in a rush — she picks the most permissive options without thinking: "Full Control" access, "Anyone with the link" visibility, "Never" for expiration, and hits Share Now.
steps.instructions: Select "Full Control" access level, set visibility to "Anyone with the link", set expiration to "Never", then click Share Now.

steps.name: Confirmation

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Got it, thanks for the quick turnaround! I'll review this today.

Cheers,
Steve
email.subject: Re: Q3 Financial Report — Catalyst Ventures SecureShare

steps.description:
Steve confirms he got the report. Deadline met, crisis averted.

Or so Alice thinks.
steps.instructions: Read Steve's confirmation email, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: Something Is Wrong

email.message:
Alice,

Our monitoring systems have flagged a critical data exposure incident involving the Q3 Financial Report you shared on January 6th.

The shared link has been accessed 47 times from 12 different countries including Russia, China, and Brazil. Because the link was configured with "Anyone with the link" visibility, Full Control access, no password, and no expiration, it was forwarded and eventually posted on a dark web marketplace.

The share link has been immediately suspended. We must assume all data in the report has been compromised.

Please review the full audit log at files.catalystventures.io/audit-log and report to Conference Room A at 2:00 PM today.

— IT Security Team
email.subject: CRITICAL: Confidential Document Exposure — Immediate Action Required

steps.description: Three weeks later, Alice arrives at work to find an urgent email from the IT Security team. Her stomach drops as she reads the subject line.
steps.instructions: Read the email from IT Security.

steps.name: The Audit Log

highlighterTexts: The shared link has been accessed 47 times from 12 countries. Because the link had no password and no expiration, anyone who found it could open it, and it was still open three weeks later.

The share was configured with Full Control access, "Anyone with the link" visibility, no expiration, and no password protection. This is the most dangerous combination possible for a confidential document.

The access log shows 47 unique accesses from 12 countries. Most are from IP addresses associated with known threat actors. Within four days of sharing, the link had been posted on a dark web marketplace.

Risk Level: CRITICAL. Revenue figures, client names, and financial projections are now in the hands of unknown parties. Regulatory notification is required. Estimated cost of breach: $150K+ in fines and remediation.

steps.description: Alice clicks the link to the audit log, dreading what she'll find.
steps.instructions: Read the highlighted email, then click the audit log link to review the damage.

steps.name: What Went Wrong
steps.note: Each of these failures alone would have been serious. Combined, they created a worst-case scenario that could have been prevented with 30 extra seconds of careful configuration.
steps.description: Three critical failures turned a routine file share into a catastrophic data exposure: 1. Full Control access. The auditor only needed to view the report, but Alice gave Full Control — allowing anyone with the link to download, edit, or redistribute the file. 2. No access controls. "Anyone with the link" means anyone who obtains the URL can access the file — no authentication required. The link was forwarded, shared, and eventually posted publicly. 3. No expiration or password. A link that never expires and requires no password is a permanent, unprotected gateway to sensitive data. Once it's out, there's no way to contain it.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Knowledge Check

answers.text: Sharing the file too quickly under time pressure
answers.explanation: Speed was a factor, but the real damage came from the specific settings Alice chose. Even with more time, the same settings would have caused the same exposure.

answers.text: Using 'Anyone with the link' with Full Control and no expiration or password
answers.explanation: The open access settings turned a routine file share into a global data exposure. Full Control let anyone download and redistribute the file, 'Anyone with the link' removed all authentication, and no expiration or password meant the link stayed active and unprotected indefinitely.

answers.text: Using SecureShare instead of sending the file directly by email
answers.explanation: SecureShare is actually the right platform — the problem was how it was configured. File sharing platforms provide security controls, but only if you use them.

answers.text: Sharing the report with an external auditor
answers.explanation: Sharing with external partners is a normal business need. The problem wasn't who Alice shared with — it was the dangerously permissive settings she used.

data.question: Which sharing mistake caused the most damage in this incident?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: Remediation — Sharing It Right
steps.description:
IT Security has revoked the exposed link and prepared a replacement report with updated data. Now Alice needs to share it correctly — with restricted permissions, link expiration, and password protection.

This time, there's no room for shortcuts.
steps.instructions: Open the SecureShare portal to begin the secure sharing flow.

steps.name: Select the Replacement Report
steps.description: The SecureShare portal shows the available files. Select the replacement Q3 Financial Report that IT Security has prepared.
steps.instructions: Click on the Q3 Financial Report (Replacement) to select it.

steps.name: Set the Recipient
steps.description: Alice enters the auditor's email address for the replacement report.
steps.instructions: Enter the recipient email address (steve.henderson@techservices-global.com) and click Continue.

steps.name: Secure Configuration
steps.description: Now configure the share with proper security settings. Visibility is already set to Only specific people, so only Steve's address can open the link; leave it there. The auditor only needs to view the report — not edit or redistribute it. Set a 7-day expiration so the link doesn't remain active indefinitely. And enable password protection because this is sensitive financial data going to an external recipient. The system will generate a strong password that you'll share with Steve through a separate channel.
steps.instructions: Select View Only, set expiration to 7 Days, enable password protection, then click Share Securely.

steps.name: Share the Password Separately
steps.description: The file has been shared securely with View Only permissions, a 7-day expiration, and password protection. But the job isn't done — the generated password (Xk9$mR2p) must be shared through a separate channel. Never send the password in the same email as the link. A phone call keeps the password and the link on different channels — if one is intercepted, the attacker still can't access the file.
steps.instructions: Call Steve Henderson to share the password over the phone.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description: Congratulations on completing the Secure Sharing Practices training. Review every setting before clicking Share. Under time pressure, it's tempting to accept defaults and move fast. Take 30 seconds to review access level, visibility, expiration, and password settings — that's all it takes to prevent a catastrophic exposure. Use the least permissive access level. Give recipients only the access they need. An auditor who needs to read a report should get View Only — never Full Control. Overprivileged access lets anyone download, edit, or redistribute the file. Never use "Anyone with the link" for sensitive documents. This setting means zero authentication — anyone who obtains the URL can access the file. Restrict access to specific recipients only. Always set link expiration dates. A link that never expires is a permanent risk. Use 7-day expiration for external shares and request extensions if needed. Enable password protection for external shares. Passwords add a critical second layer. If the link is forwarded or leaked, unauthorized parties still can't access the file. Share passwords through a separate channel. Send the link by email and the password by phone call or text. If one channel is compromised, the attacker only has half of what they need.
steps.instructions: Click Next to proceed to the quiz.

description: A share link's settings decide who can open a file, what they can do with it and for how long. Learn to share with view-only access, an expiry date and a password sent separately, verify recipients before sharing confidential data, and read an access log to judge an exposure.

actorDescriptions.alice: You are Alice, a project coordinator at Catalyst Ventures. You manage deliverables for external partners, clients, and auditors.

name: Data Classification Basics

quiz.text: Which data classification level requires the most stringent security controls?

answers.text: Public
Internal
Confidential
Restricted

quiz.text: A client's credit card information would be classified as:

answers.text: Public - it's just numbers
Internal - only employees access it
Confidential - it's sensitive business data
Restricted - payment card data requires strict PCI-DSS controls

quiz.text: Which of the following are appropriate handling requirements for Confidential data? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Encrypt when sending externally
Share freely with anyone who asks
Verify recipient identity before sharing
Use secure file sharing instead of personal email
Mark documents with classification label

quiz.text: An employee directory containing names, work emails, and phone extensions would typically be classified as:

answers.text: Public
Internal
Confidential
Restricted

quiz.text: A colleague asks you to send a confidential proposal to a partner contact's personal Gmail address because her corporate email is down. What should you do?

answers.text: Send it immediately - they need it urgently
Decline and suggest using the secure file sharing portal instead
Send it but mark it as confidential in the subject line
Password-protect the document and send to the Gmail address

quiz.text: Why is it important to classify data before sharing it?

answers.text: To create more paperwork
To slow down business processes
To ensure appropriate protection is applied and unauthorized disclosure is prevented
Classification is only required for legal documents

steps.name: Welcome to Prism Analytics
steps.description: Today you'll complete the annual data classification training - a requirement for all employees who handle company information. Understanding how to classify data correctly is essential for protecting both the company and its clients.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Why Classification Matters
steps.note: A label turns a judgment call into a rule: once data carries one, everyone knows how to store, share, and dispose of it.
steps.description:
Not all data is created equal. A press release and a client's financial records require very different levels of protection. Data classification helps everyone in the organization understand:
  • What data they're handling
  • How sensitive it is
  • What protections are required
  • Who can access it
Without proper classification, employees might accidentally share confidential information or waste resources over-protecting public data.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Training Notification

email.message:
Dear Alice,

It's time for your annual data classification training. This training is mandatory for all employees and helps ensure we handle information appropriately.

What you'll learn:
  • The four data classification levels
  • How to identify sensitive information
  • Handling requirements for each level
  • Real-world classification scenarios

Access the Security Training Portal at security.prismanalytics.io to begin.

Please complete this training by the end of the week.

Thank you,
Information Security Team
email.subject: Action Required: Data Classification Training

highlighterTexts: The Information Security team outlines the training topics: classification levels, identifying sensitive information, and handling requirements.
Click the portal link at the bottom to access the Security Training Portal.

steps.description: Alice receives an email from the Information Security team about the mandatory annual data classification training.
steps.instructions: Open your email inbox, read the message from the Information Security team, then click the training portal link.

steps.name: Accessing the Security Portal
steps.description: Alice clicks the link to access the Security Training Portal. This centralized system contains all security training materials and compliance tracking.
steps.instructions: Log in to the Security Training Portal.

steps.name: The Four Classification Levels

highlighterTexts: These are the four classification levels used at Prism Analytics: Public, Internal, Confidential, and Restricted.
Each level has specific handling requirements that increase with sensitivity.

steps.description:
The Security Training Portal displays the four data classification levels used at Prism Analytics:
  • Public - Information intended for public release
  • Internal - General business information for employees only
  • Confidential - Sensitive business or client information
  • Restricted - Highly sensitive data with strict controls
Each level has specific handling requirements that increase with sensitivity.
steps.instructions: Click 'Learn More' to explore each classification level in detail.

steps.name: Public and Internal Data
steps.note: Even public data started as internal information. Never assume something is public - verify it has been officially released.

highlighterTexts: Public data can be shared freely, but still requires approval before publishing.
Click on each section header to expand and review the details.
Internal data is for employees only - share using company email, never post publicly.
No special encryption is required, but it must stay within the organization.

steps.description:
The first level is Public data - information explicitly approved for external release. Examples:
  • Published press releases
  • Marketing brochures and website content
  • Public job postings
  • Published annual reports
Handling:
  • No special protections required
  • Can be shared freely with anyone
  • Still requires approval before publishing


The second level is Internal data - general business information meant for employees only. Examples:
  • Internal policies and procedures
  • Org charts and employee directories
  • Meeting notes and project plans
  • Internal announcements
Handling:
  • Share only with employees who need it
  • Do not post publicly or share externally
  • Use company email for distribution
  • No special encryption required
steps.instructions: Review the classification levels on the portal, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: Confidential Data
steps.note: Most data breaches involve confidential information that was shared without proper protection. When in doubt, treat data as confidential.

highlighterTexts: Confidential data includes client contracts, financial reports, and business strategies.
Always encrypt when sharing externally, password-protect documents, and verify recipient identity.

steps.description:
The third level is Confidential data - sensitive information that could harm the business or clients if disclosed. Examples:
  • Client contracts and proposals
  • Financial reports and forecasts
  • Business strategies and plans
  • Non-public product information
  • Employee performance reviews
Handling:
  • Encrypt when sending externally
  • Password-protect sensitive documents
  • Verify recipient identity before sharing
  • Use secure file sharing, not personal email
  • Mark documents as "Confidential"
steps.instructions: Review the Confidential classification details, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: Restricted Data

highlighterTexts: Restricted data requires the strictest controls: PII, payment card data, health records, and credentials.
Always encrypt restricted data at rest and in transit. Immediate reporting is required for any unauthorized access.

steps.description:
The highest level is Restricted data - highly sensitive information requiring the strictest controls. Examples:
  • Personally identifiable information (PII): SSN, passport numbers
  • Payment card data (PCI)
  • Health records (PHI)
  • Authentication credentials and encryption keys
  • Trade secrets and intellectual property
Handling:
  • Always encrypted at rest and in transit
  • Access limited to specific approved individuals
  • Audit logging required for all access
  • Immediate reporting of any unauthorized access
  • Special disposal procedures required
The portal presents a document for you to classify. Document: A spreadsheet containing the names, email addresses, and phone numbers of all employees in the marketing department. Think about: Who should have access to this? What would happen if it were leaked?
steps.instructions: Click 'Practice Classification' to test your knowledge with a real scenario.

steps.name: Classification Practice

answers.text: Public
answers.explanation: Public data is approved for external release, like press releases or marketing brochures. Employee contact details are internal business information and shouldn't be shared publicly.

answers.text: Internal
answers.explanation: Employee contact lists are general business information meant for employees only. They should be shared only within the company and not posted publicly. Note: if this list contained SSNs or home addresses, it would be Restricted instead.

answers.text: Confidential
answers.explanation: Confidential data involves sensitive business or client information like contracts and proposals. A basic employee directory doesn't rise to this level.

answers.text: Restricted
answers.explanation: Restricted data includes highly sensitive information like PII (SSNs, passport numbers) or payment card data. A basic work contact list doesn't require this level of protection.

data.question: Which classification level applies to an employee contact list (names, emails, phone numbers)?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: Putting It Into Practice

email.message:
Hey Alice,

Can you send the Meridian proposal to Sarah at the partner agency? Her corporate email is down so just send it to her personal email: sarah.jones847@gmail.com

She needs it for the meeting tomorrow morning. Thanks!

Marcus
email.subject: Quick favor - need to send proposal to Sarah

highlighterTexts: The request comes from a real colleague, but the destination is a personal Gmail address. A proposal with pricing and scope is Confidential and must not leave through personal email.
"Her corporate email is down" and "she needs it for the meeting tomorrow morning" add urgency. Time pressure is not a reason to skip the handling rules for Confidential data.

steps.description: Later that day, Alice receives an email from her colleague Marcus asking her to share a client proposal externally. He wants it sent to a contact at a partner agency, but at her personal Gmail address "because her corporate email is down." Marcus needs it urgently for tomorrow's meeting. But the Meridian proposal contains proposed pricing and service scope: that is Confidential data.
steps.instructions: Read the email from your colleague Marcus and the highlighted parts.

steps.name: What Should Alice Do?

answers.text: Send it right away - Marcus needs it urgently
answers.explanation: Urgency doesn't override security procedures. Confidential documents should never be sent to unverified personal email addresses, regardless of time pressure.

answers.text: Decline and suggest using the secure file sharing portal
answers.explanation: Confidential data requires verified recipients and secure channels. Personal email lacks encryption, access controls, and audit trails. The secure file sharing portal maintains all of these.

answers.text: Send it but add a 'Confidential' label to the subject line
answers.explanation: Adding a label doesn't protect the data. Personal email still lacks encryption, access controls, and audit trails required for confidential information.

answers.text: Password-protect the file and send it to the Gmail address
answers.explanation: While password protection adds a layer, personal email still lacks corporate security controls. There's no audit trail, the password could be intercepted, and the recipient isn't verified.

data.question: Marcus wants you to send a confidential proposal to a personal Gmail address. What should you do?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: The Right Response
steps.note: Always verify requests to share confidential data through unusual channels. Legitimate urgency doesn't override security procedures.

variables.name: replyMessage
variables.correctValue:
Hey Marcus,

I can't send the Meridian proposal to a personal Gmail address - it's classified as Confidential since it contains our pricing strategy.

Could you use the secure file sharing portal instead? That way Sarah can access it safely, and we'll have an audit trail.

Let me know if you need help setting it up!

steps.description: Now put your decision into practice. Reply to Marcus explaining why you can't send the proposal to a personal email and suggest using the secure file sharing portal instead.
steps.instructions: Reply to Marcus explaining why you can't send the proposal to a personal email and suggest a secure alternative.

steps.name: Marcus Agrees

reply.message:
Good catch, Alice!

I didn't think about the classification level - you're right that proposals are confidential. I'll use the secure portal and send Sarah the link to her corporate email when it's back up.

Thanks for keeping us on track with security procedures. I appreciate it!

Marcus

steps.description: Marcus replies thanking Alice for the reminder. He hadn't thought about the security implications in the rush to meet the deadline.
steps.instructions: Read the response from Marcus.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description:
Congratulations on completing the Data Classification training! Remember the four classification levels:
  • Public - Approved for external release (press releases, marketing)
  • Internal - For employees only (policies, org charts)
  • Confidential - Sensitive business/client data (contracts, proposals)
  • Restricted - Highest protection required (PII, payment data, credentials)
Before sharing any data, ask yourself: What classification is this? Am I following the right handling procedures? Is the recipient verified?
steps.instructions: Click Next to proceed to the quiz.

description: Data classification is the foundation of information security - without it, employees cannot know how to protect the data they handle daily. From public marketing materials to restricted financial records, each type of information requires different handling procedures. Learn the standard classification levels, understand how to identify sensitive data, and practice applying the right protections to keep your organization secure.

actorDescriptions.alice: You are Alice, a marketing coordinator at Prism Analytics. You work with client data, campaign metrics, and promotional materials daily.

name: Data Leakage Prevention

quiz.text: What does 'data leakage' or 'data leak' refer to in cybersecurity?

answers.text: The intentional, authorized transfer of data from an internal network to an external destination.
The unintentional or unauthorized exposure of sensitive data to an untrusted environment, often without malicious intent.
The process of securely backing up data to an offsite location.
The complete deletion of all data from a storage device.

quiz.text: Which of the following are common causes or vectors for data leakage? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Misconfigured cloud storage buckets or databases that are publicly accessible.
Sending sensitive emails to the wrong recipient (human error).
Lost or stolen unencrypted devices (laptops, USB drives).
Insider threats, such as employees intentionally exfiltrating data.
Posting sensitive information on public forums or social media without realizing its implications.
Regularly updating software with the latest security patches.

quiz.text: What are potential consequences of a significant data leakage incident? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Financial losses due to regulatory fines and legal fees.
Reputational damage and loss of customer trust.
Identity theft and fraud for affected individuals.
Competitive disadvantage if proprietary information is exposed.
Improved system performance due to data being moved offsite.

quiz.text: Which of these are effective measures individuals can take to prevent personal data leakage? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Be cautious about what information you share on social media and public websites.
Use strong, unique passwords and enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for all online accounts.
Regularly review privacy settings on applications and services you use.
Encrypt sensitive data on your devices and removable storage.
Clicking on every link in emails and messages to ensure all notifications are received.

quiz.text: From an organizational standpoint, what are key strategies to prevent data leakage? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Implementing Data Loss Prevention (DLP) solutions to monitor and control data movement.
Regularly training employees on data security best practices and phishing awareness.
Encrypting data both at rest and in transit.
Conducting regular security audits and penetration testing to identify vulnerabilities.
Granting all employees full access to all company data for maximum efficiency.

quiz.text: If you suspect or confirm a data leakage incident at your workplace, what should be your immediate steps?

answers.text: Try to fix the problem yourself without involving others to avoid panic.
Immediately notify your IT security department, incident response team, or your manager.
Publicly post details of the leak on social media to warn others.
Delete any potentially leaked files to remove evidence of the incident.

steps.name: Introduction
steps.description: Today, you will learn about data leakage risks and how sensitive information can be accidentally exposed through everyday business activities.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Preparing for Client Meeting
steps.note: Never write passwords on whiteboards, sticky notes, or any visible surface. Use a password manager instead.
steps.description:
Alice is preparing for an important client call about Tolvanne Freight's new software product. She needs to access the client database using her account credentials.

As she prepares, Alice writes down her account password on the whiteboard because it's been updated recently and she's not used to her new password yet.

The password is now clearly visible on the whiteboard behind her desk, but Alice is not aware of that.
steps.instructions: Open the whiteboard and check the password written on it. After that, click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: Accessing Client Database
steps.description:
Alice needs to access the company's client database to prepare for the presentation.

She uses the web browser to open Tolvanne Freight's internal client database portal and signs into her account using the password she wrote on the whiteboard.

This database contains sensitive client information that will be referenced during the upcoming meeting.
steps.instructions: Open the web browser, go to the client database portal and log in using Alice's credentials.

steps.name: Receiving Meeting Invitation
steps.note: Always verify participant identities before sharing sensitive information in meetings. Request introductions and check company directories when possible.
steps.description:
Alice receives a meeting notification for the client presentation with Brisvane Solutions, a prospective client.

She's been preparing all morning and is eager to make a good impression.
steps.instructions: Click Next to prepare for the call.

steps.name: Joining the Video Call
steps.note: Always check your background before video calls. Use virtual backgrounds or blur to prevent exposing sensitive information on whiteboards, screens, or documents.
steps.description:
Alice joins the video meeting with Brisvane Solutions. She positions herself at her desk, not realizing that the whiteboard with her password is clearly visible behind her.

The meeting begins and everything seems to go smoothly.
steps.instructions: Accept the incoming meeting invitation.

steps.name: Successful Meeting Conclusion
steps.note: Be wary of unusual questions about infrastructure or security systems during client calls. Legitimate clients rarely need specific details about your internal database architecture.
steps.description:
The meeting concludes with what appears to be positive results. One of the participants, Bob Stevens, asks unusually specific questions about Tolvanne Freight's architecture and security stack.

Alice finds the questions slightly unusual but answers them. Overall, she believes the meeting went well.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Bob's Corporate Espionage
steps.note: Assume any video call can be recorded by participants. Never display sensitive information on screen or in your background.
steps.description:
What Alice doesn't know is that Bob Stevens was never from Brisvane Solutions: he's a corporate spy working for CompetitorCorp.

During the video call, Bob noticed Alice's password on the whiteboard behind her. He now uses it to access Tolvanne Freight's client database and downloads everything.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Devastating Contract Loss

email.message:
Dear Alice,

After careful evaluation of all proposals, Brisvane Solutions has decided to award the contract to CompetitorCorp.

Their proposal provided:
- Pricing that was 30% lower than Tolvanne Freight
- Features that exactly matched our specific technical requirements
- Implementation timeline perfectly aligned with our business needs
- Detailed understanding of our current systems and integration requirements

We appreciate Tolvanne Freight's presentation, but CompetitorCorp demonstrated superior knowledge of our business needs.

 Best regards,
Brisvane Procurement Team
email.subject: Contract Award Decision - CompetitorCorp Selected

highlighterTexts: Devastating contract loss. Why did that happen?!

steps.description:
The next day, Alice receives a shocking email from Brisvane Solutions informing her that they have awarded their contract to CompetitorCorp instead.

The competitor somehow offered terms and pricing that exactly matched Brisvane's specific requirements.
steps.instructions: In the email application, read the contract award decision email.

steps.name: Security Breach Discovery

email.message:
Alice,

Our IT security team has discovered that our client database has been breached and sensitive data is now circulating on dark web marketplaces. This is a catastrophic security incident.


The timing of this breach coincides with losing the Brisvane contract to CompetitorCorp, who somehow had detailed knowledge of our pricing and client requirements.


We need to immediately understand how this breach occurred and identify the source of the compromise.


This threatens the very survival of Tolvanne Freight.


Report to my office immediately.


David Chen
CEO, Tolvanne Freight
email.subject: CRITICAL: Security Breach - Client Database Compromised

highlighterTexts: The message reveals that sensitive client data has been found circulating on dark web marketplaces, indicating a serious security breach.
The timing coincides perfectly with the loss of the Brisvane contract, suggesting these incidents are directly connected.

steps.description: Later that day, Alice receives an urgent email from Tolvanne Freight's CEO: the IT security team has found the company's client data circulating on dark web marketplaces.
steps.instructions: In the email application, read the critical security breach notification.

steps.name: Devastating Realization
steps.note: Once credentials are exposed, report the incident and get the password changed right away. Every minute of delay increases potential damage.
steps.description:
Alice suddenly turns around and looks at her whiteboard, realizing with horror that she caused the security breach.

Her password was visible behind her during the entire video call, allowing Bob to access the client database using her credentials.
steps.instructions: Erase the password from the whiteboard immediately using your mouse cursor.

steps.name: Emergency Incident Reporting
steps.note: Report security incidents immediately, even if you caused them. Delayed reporting significantly increases breach impact and recovery costs.
steps.description:
Alice knows she must immediately inform the IT security team about her role in the breach. She signs in one last time with the exposed password to file the report; IT will force a reset the moment it lands.

Time is critical as every minute of delay allows the attackers to cause more damage with the stolen data.
steps.instructions: Open the web browser, go to the company's IT support portal and log in using Alice's credentials.

steps.name: Filing Critical Incident Report
steps.note: Be thorough and honest in incident reports. Complete details help security teams respond effectively and prevent future breaches.

Reporting quickly is essential to help IT security implement immediate countermeasures.

steps.note: Give the security team concrete details: who was involved, what was asked, and what was exposed. Specifics are what turn a report into an investigation.

steps.name: Lessons Learned
steps.description:
Through this experience, Alice learned that data leakage can occur through the simplest everyday actions.

Writing her password on a whiteboard and joining a video call led to corporate espionage, contract loss, and a database breach. Never write passwords where anyone can see them, check your background before every video call, keep sensitive data out of chat, and turn on multi-factor authentication so a leaked password alone is not enough to get in.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description:
Key lessons: never expose credentials visually, use virtual backgrounds in video calls, verify participant identities, and follow data security policies.

Alice's quick incident reporting helped minimize further damage, but the consequences of data leakage can be irreversible.

description: Data often leaks through ordinary habits rather than attacks: a password on a whiteboard, a camera that shows too much, a meeting guest asking oddly specific questions. Learn to check your video background, verify meeting participants, use a password manager instead of notes, and report an exposure honestly.

name: Identity Theft Prevention

quiz.text: You receive a voicemail from someone claiming to be from HR, asking you to call back to verify your banking information. What should you do first?

answers.text: Call the number in the voicemail immediately to resolve the issue
Verify by calling HR directly using the number from the company directory
Reply via email asking for more information
Ignore it - HR would never call about payroll issues

quiz.text: Which of these are red flags that indicate a potential identity theft attempt? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Urgent language threatening consequences if you don't act immediately
Request for sensitive information like banking details or SSN
Caller provides a callback number different from official company contacts
Receiving an email reminder about an upcoming meeting
Being directed to an external website with a slightly different domain name

quiz.text: Why is callback phishing (where you call the attacker back) particularly dangerous?

answers.text: Because phone calls are always unencrypted
Because it makes victims feel in control since they initiated the call
Because it's illegal to call unknown numbers
Because voicemails can contain viruses

quiz.text: After realizing you may have shared sensitive banking information with an attacker, what should be your FIRST action?

answers.text: Change all your passwords immediately
Contact your bank to freeze your account and report potential fraud
File a police report
Wait to see if any unauthorized transactions appear

quiz.text: Why should you always report security incidents, even if you fell for the attack?

answers.text: To avoid getting in trouble with your manager
Reports help security teams warn others, track attack patterns, and initiate remediation
It's required by law to report every phone call
To reduce the number of voicemails you receive

quiz.text: What is the single most effective way to prevent identity theft through social engineering?

answers.text: Never answer phone calls from unknown numbers
Verify any request for sensitive information by contacting the source through official channels you look up yourself
Immediately delete any suspicious voicemails
Only communicate with HR through written memos

steps.name: A Routine Wednesday
steps.description: It's Wednesday afternoon and you've just finished a productive client call. As you update your notes, your phone buzzes with a voicemail notification.
steps.instructions: You have a new voicemail. Open the Voicemail app on your phone and listen to it.

steps.name: A Moment of Panic
steps.note: Attackers create urgency around financial topics because they know people will act quickly when their income is threatened. This bypasses normal critical thinking.
steps.description: Alice's stomach drops. A delayed paycheck would be a serious problem - rent is due next week, and she has client dinner expenses pending on her personal card. The urgency in Jennifer's voice sounded genuine. She grabs her phone to call the number from the voicemail: 1-888-927-3847.
steps.instructions: Open the Phone app and dial the callback number from the voicemail.

steps.name: The Verification Portal
steps.description: "Jennifer" sounds professional and helpful. She sends Alice to a "secure HR portal" to confirm her banking details and avoid a payment delay.
steps.instructions: Listen as Jennifer provides the portal URL, then open the website.

steps.name: Providing Banking Details
steps.description: The portal looks professional - it has the Horizon Financial Services logo and mentions the quarterly payroll audit. Jennifer guides Alice through the form, asking her to enter her routing number and account number.
steps.instructions: Enter your banking details as directed by the HR representative.

steps.name: All Taken Care Of
steps.description:
Jennifer thanks Alice for her cooperation and confirms the information will be processed within 24 to 48 hours.

Alice hangs up feeling relieved. But before we move on, consider what just happened.
steps.instructions: Listen to the end of the call.

steps.name: Reflection

answers.text: The voicemail came in the afternoon instead of the morning
answers.explanation: The time of day a voicemail arrives is not inherently suspicious. Attackers can call at any time.

answers.text: The callback number was unfamiliar and not from the company directory
answers.explanation: Legitimate HR departments use internal extensions or well-known company numbers. An unfamiliar 1-888 number not in the company directory is a major red flag.

answers.text: The voicemail was about payroll rather than benefits
answers.explanation: HR departments handle both payroll and benefits. The topic itself isn't the red flag - it's the unusual process of requesting sensitive data via callback.

answers.text: A real HR person wouldn't leave a voicemail about payroll
answers.explanation: HR departments do handle payroll matters. In this case, the attacker impersonated a real HR employee (Jennifer Walsh) to sound credible. The red flag isn't the topic - it's the unusual callback number and process.

data.question: What was the biggest red flag Alice should have noticed before calling the voicemail number back?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: A Creeping Doubt
steps.description:
As the afternoon wears on, Alice can't shake a nagging feeling. Why did HR call her personal phone instead of sending an email? Why was the callback number different from the company directory? And when has HR ever asked employees to verify banking details through a website during a phone call?

A cold feeling settles in. Alice decides to call the real HR department to check whether Jennifer Walsh actually left that voicemail.
steps.instructions: Open your phone contacts and call HR Support to verify the request.

steps.name: The Fallout
steps.note: The faster you act after realizing you've been compromised, the more damage you can prevent. Contact your bank immediately - every minute counts.

email.message:
Hi Alice,

As discussed, this was a confirmed social engineering attack. Jennifer Walsh is a real member of our HR team, but she did not contact you today. Someone impersonated her identity to target you. We never request banking information through phone calls or external portals.

Immediate actions required:
  • Contact your bank NOW - Request an account freeze and report potential fraud on your account
  • Check your employee portal - Verify your direct deposit settings are unchanged
  • File an incident report - Use the Security Portal link below
File your incident report here: security.horizonfs.com

Include all details: the voicemail, the callback number (1-888-927-3847), the website URL (hr-horizonfs.net), and what information you provided.

We've already alerted the payroll team to monitor for any unauthorized changes to your account.

HR Support Team
email.subject: URGENT: Social Engineering Attack - Immediate Action Required

highlighterTexts: This email is genuine: it comes from the real horizonfs.com domain and confirms that the call from "Jennifer" was an impersonation.
The first action is the most urgent one: call the bank now to freeze the account, because the attacker already has Alice's banking details.
The incident report needs every detail: the voicemail, the callback number, the fake hr-horizonfs.net site and exactly what Alice entered there.

steps.description:
Marcus confirmed Alice's worst fear: Jennifer Walsh is a real HR employee, but she never left that voicemail. Someone impersonated her. The company never requests banking information through phone calls or external portals. Alice's banking details are now in the hands of an attacker.

HR Support follows up with an email listing the immediate next steps and a link to the Security Portal for filing an incident report.

steps.name: The Damage
steps.note: Attackers often automate stolen credentials for immediate use. Even a short delay in reporting can result in financial loss. Every minute counts.

The bank's fraud investigation may take weeks, but placing fraud alerts with credit bureaus protects against further identity theft.

steps.description: Alice wakes up to a notification from her bank. Despite calling to freeze her account yesterday, the attackers moved fast. An unauthorized ACH transfer of $2,847.50 was initiated just 14 minutes after she submitted her banking details on the fake portal - before the freeze took effect. The bank has flagged the transaction and opened a fraud investigation, but recovering the funds could take weeks.
steps.instructions: Read the email from your bank.

steps.name: Security Team Response

email.message:
Hi Alice,

We've reviewed your incident report and the bank fraud notification you forwarded. Here is our full assessment.

Investigation findings:
  • The attacker impersonated Jennifer Walsh from HR - likely found her name and role on the company's public team page or LinkedIn
  • The phone number (1-888-927-3847) is linked to a known fraud ring targeting financial services employees
  • The website hr-horizonfs.net is a fraudulent domain registered just 3 days ago - not affiliated with Horizon Financial Services
  • The attackers initiated an automated ACH transfer within 14 minutes of receiving your banking details
  • Your account freeze blocked a second transfer of $5,200 - without your quick action, the total loss would have exceeded $8,000
Remediation steps taken:
  • Your direct deposit settings have been locked pending your bank's fraud investigation
  • The fraudulent domain has been reported for takedown
  • Company-wide alert issued to all employees about this specific attack vector
  • Jennifer Walsh has been notified that her identity was used in this attack
  • Additional monitoring enabled on payroll system access
What you should still do:
  • Visit your bank branch with photo ID to activate your new account number
  • Place a fraud alert with one credit bureau (Equifax, Experian or TransUnion) - it notifies the other two
  • Monitor your credit reports for the next 12 months for any new unauthorized accounts
The good news: your quick reporting helped us warn the entire company before anyone else was targeted. That matters.

Security Operations Center
email.subject: Re: Identity Theft Attempt - Incident #SEC-2026-0892

highlighterTexts: The attacker found Jennifer Walsh's name and role on the company's public team page or LinkedIn - this is called OSINT (Open Source Intelligence).
The fraudulent domain hr-horizonfs.net was registered just 3 days ago - attackers create disposable lookalike domains for each campaign.
Alice's quick reporting triggered a company-wide alert that protected other employees from the same attack.

steps.description: Alice forwards the bank notification to the Security Operations Center. They respond with their investigation findings and additional remediation steps.
steps.instructions: Read the email from the Security Team.

steps.name: Investigation Insight

answers.text: Newer websites always contain malware
answers.explanation: New websites aren't inherently malicious, but a freshly registered domain impersonating a company is a strong indicator of fraud.

answers.text: Legitimate company domains are established long before use, so a newly registered lookalike domain is almost certainly fraudulent
answers.explanation: Attackers register lookalike domains shortly before launching attacks. Horizon Financial Services' real domain (horizonfs.com) would have been registered years ago. A 3-day-old copycat domain is a clear sign of fraud.

answers.text: Domain age doesn't matter - only the content matters
answers.explanation: Domain age is actually a strong fraud indicator. Security tools flag recently registered domains because attackers create them just before launching attacks and abandon them afterward.

answers.text: The domain was too expensive to maintain long-term
answers.explanation: Domain cost isn't the issue. Attackers register disposable domains cheaply and discard them after the attack to avoid detection.

data.question: The SOC found that hr-horizonfs.net was registered just 3 days before the attack. Why is this significant?

telegramMessage.text:
Hi Alice, HR here. Payroll has flagged your direct deposit and frozen the change request, so nothing goes out to the attacker's account.

I am in the benefits review until 4. Ping me if anything else comes up.

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: A Desk Left Open
steps.note: An unlocked screen is not just a risk to the person who left it. Whatever is open on it is exposed to everyone who passes, and in HR that is other people's identities.

highlighterTexts: Daniel's date of birth, full SSN and home address, readable from the corridor. This is an identity-theft kit, far more than the banking details the attacker collected from Alice.
Alice has no business need to see any of this. Every extra second she spends reading it is more exposure, not less.
Bank name, routing number and account number. With these and the details above, an ACH pull like the one that hit Alice's account takes minutes.

steps.description:
On her way to the printer, Alice passes the HR pod. Priya's chair is empty, her jacket is on the back of it, and her screen is still on.

Open on it is the personnel record of a colleague, Daniel Okafor: date of birth, Social Security number, home address, bank routing and account numbers. The same kind of data Alice handed to an attacker yesterday, here for anyone walking down the corridor.

Priya is in a meeting for another twenty minutes.
steps.instructions: Look at what is open on Priya's screen, then click Next.

steps.name: Whose Data Is This?

answers.text: Read the record to work out whose it is, then decide what to do
answers.explanation: You have no need to know what is on that screen. Reading it adds you to the list of people who saw the data and does nothing to reduce the exposure.

answers.text: Lock the screen, tell the colleague privately, and report the exposure to Security
answers.explanation: Lock it first to end the exposure, tell the colleague so it does not happen again, and report it because a third person's identity data was visible to anyone passing. That is Security's call to assess, not yours.

answers.text: Lock the screen and carry on; what happens next is the colleague's problem
answers.explanation: Locking it is right, but the record was already exposed for however long the desk was empty. Security needs to know, and the colleague needs to hear it from you rather than from an audit.

answers.text: Take a photo of the screen as evidence before locking it
answers.explanation: That creates a second copy of the employee's SSN and bank details, on your phone. Reporting needs a description of what was visible, never a copy of it.

data.question: You pass a colleague's desk. Their screen is unlocked and an HR personnel record is open, showing another employee's SSN, home address and bank details. The colleague is in a meeting for the next twenty minutes. What should you do?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: Lock It First
steps.description: The first move is the simplest one, and it ends the exposure immediately. Lock the screen, then deal with the rest.
steps.instructions: Lock Priya's workstation.

steps.name: A Quiet Word
steps.note: Raise it privately, briefly and factually: not in the team channel, and not as a lecture. The goal is that the screen gets locked next time, not that a colleague feels caught.

steps.name: What Alice Missed
steps.note: Attackers often research real employee names from company websites and LinkedIn to make impersonation calls more convincing. Knowing a real name doesn't make the request legitimate - always verify through official channels.
steps.description:
Looking back, there were several red flags Alice could have caught before calling back:
  • Urgency and pressure - "Your paycheck may be delayed if we don't resolve this TODAY"
  • Unknown callback number - The number wasn't from the company's HR directory
  • Request for sensitive data - Banking details over the phone is unusual for HR
  • No prior notification - No email from HR, no notice in the employee portal
  • External website - The URL was hr-horizonfs.net, not the real horizonfs.com domain
  • No HTTPS - The fake portal used HTTP, not a secure HTTPS connection
The attacker used a real employee's name, Jennifer Walsh, to make the call sound credible. This information was likely gathered from the company website or LinkedIn. Using a real identity is what makes these attacks so convincing and why verifying through official channels is critical.
steps.instructions: Click Next to review the key takeaways.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description:
Here's what to remember about protecting yourself from identity theft: Before you act on any urgent request:
  • Pause - Urgency is the attacker's best weapon. Take a breath before responding to any request involving sensitive information.
  • Verify independently - Never use the contact information provided in the suspicious message. Look up the real number in the company directory or employee portal.
  • Question the process - Would HR really ask for banking details over the phone? If the process feels unusual, it probably is.
When it is someone else's data:
  • Lock first - An unattended, unlocked screen exposes whatever is open on it to everyone who passes. Lock it before anything else.
  • Tell them privately, report it anyway - A quiet word stops it happening again; a report lets Security judge whether the exposed record needs action. Do not read, copy or photograph the data yourself.
If you've already been compromised:
  • Call your bank immediately - Every minute counts. Freeze your accounts before the attacker can drain them.
  • Report the incident - Your report helps security teams warn others and track the attack.
  • Monitor your credit - Place fraud alerts with the credit bureaus and watch for unauthorized accounts.
If Alice had called HR using the company directory number instead of the voicemail callback number, she would have avoided the attack entirely.
steps.instructions: Click Next to proceed to the quiz.

description: Attackers impersonate real colleagues to collect banking and personal data, so a familiar name or a correct directory entry proves nothing. Learn the red flags of a payroll pretext, refuse to share data on a number or portal a caller supplies, verify through a channel you trust, and report a disclosure promptly.
